Title: Pure Thermo Poison: Why 35 Countries Build the World ’ s Largest Thermonuclear Reactor

Content: Pure Thermo Poison: Why 35 countries are building the world ’ s largest thermonuclear reactor The U.S.-USSR Summit in 1985 gave the world one of the most ambitious technological projects: the experimental thermonuclear reactor ITER ("path").
In Provence, in southern France, thousands of scientists and builders are preparing a complex for scientific experiments that can open the way for humanity to the thermonuclear power plants of the future.
Thermonuclear synthesis has long stirred minds.
In theory, such power plants can be four times more efficient than modern nuclear power plants, much cleaner and safer.
They have no problems with uncontrolled chain reactions and highly radioactive waste, and marine water can be used as fuel.
The EU (46% of expenses), the USA, Russia, India, China, South Korea and Japan (each – 9%) work on a multi-billion dollar project.
If there are no further delays and funding problems, ITER will start working at the end of 2025 – 40 years after the talks between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev in Geneva.
The present time tells about the history, present and future of a unique project in the field of thermonuclear synthesis.
How does thermonuclear energy work is trying to copy the processes that occur inside the stars: there, at ultra-high temperatures and pressure, the nuclei of hydrogen isotopes merge and emit huge energy.
To achieve this on Earth, special conditions are necessary (for example, the temperature is 10 times higher than in the core of the Sun) - they are created in a thermonuclear reactor.
It is based at least on the most common scheme used by ITER – tokamak, shaped like a bagel vacuum chamber with magnetic coils.
The first tokamaks appeared in the USSR in the 1960s, for ITER will build the largest tokamak in the world with a volume of 830 m3.
In tokamak, deuterium and tritium are launched, and heated to temperatures over 150 million degrees Celsius.
The gas turns into a plasma, and so that the plasma of this temperature does not burn all around, it is held at a distance from the walls by a magnetic field; through the plasma itself, a current is passed.
A powerful magnetic field is provided, in turn, by superconducting magnets, which need to be cooled in a vacuum chamber to almost absolute zero – 268 ° C.
Physically, they will be literally half a meter from the hot plasma to 150,000,000 ° C.
Ensuring trouble-free operation of equipment in such conditions is a complex engineering task.
Modern tokamaki emit less energy than it is spent on heating the system, it is not yet possible to adapt them to generate them.
The best result is the British JET, which returns up to 67% of the energy spent.
Due to the size of the ITER structure (it will be a giant with a height of a nine-storey house, and about the same diameter), the creators expect that the reactor will be able to allocate energy ten times more than it is spent on plasma heating (to give 500 MW from 50 MW).
This point is fundamental for the construction of thermonuclear power plants in the future.
But ITER will not produce electricity: all the allocated energy will only be spent on heating the walls of the tokamak.
Although if the experiments with ITER are successful, the next stage (from 2030) will be the prototype of a thermonuclear reactor for power plants, DEMO – they should appear in the 2040-50s.
India, Russia, South Korea and Japan expressed their desire to build such reactors.
The most important goal of ITER is to show the possibility of generating energy by a thermonuclear reactor.
This will require the controlled production of "burning plasma" (with it the synthesis reaction will be self-sustaining) and the self-reproduction of tritium, a rather rare isotope used as fuel.
In addition, ITER should demonstrate how modern technologies are ready for the construction of commercial thermonuclear power plants, as well as assess their reliability and safety.
Safety is one of the key advantages of thermonuclear reactors over conventional nuclear ones.
There is no chain reaction with consequences: in case of plasma problems, it will instantly cool down and fade, ITER notes.
What is better with the radioactivity of the fuel: tritium, a weak source of beta radiation, will be generated directly in the reactor.
The design of the reactor involves several barriers to radioactive substances arising during operation.
The half-life of radioactive waste for most isotopes in a thermonuclear reactor is about 10 years, whereas for individual components of spent nuclear fuel these values can be thousands or even millions of years.
From zero to 63% In November 1985, at a meeting in Geneva, the leaders of the United States and the USSR agreed on a joint study of thermonuclear energy for peaceful purposes – this was the beginning of the project.
A year later, he was Euroate, the USSR, the United States and Japan.
Work on the ITER design began in 1988 and continued until the final version was approved in 2001.
In 2003, China and South Korea joined the ITER consortium, and India joined the ITER consortium in 2005.
At the same time, a place for construction was chosen: the vicinity of Saint-Paul-les-Durants in Provence, France, near the research center for nuclear power Kadarash.
The Inter-State Agreement on the Establishment of ITER was signed by the Ministers of the participating countries on November 21, 2006, and in October 2007, ITER Organization, a legal entity responsible for the construction, operation and subsequent dismantling of the reactor, began its work.
The site began to cook in 2007, build - in 2010.
In parallel, the participating countries began to work on the elements of the ITER complex: India is building a cryostat for the project, the US is developing a central magnetic coil (its strength is enough to lift the aircraft carrier), the EU and Korea are preparing a vacuum chamber, China and Russia supply superconductors (a total of 100,000 km of such conductors), part of the coils and various electrical components, Japan is preparing toroidal field coils.
As of the end of June 2019, the project was ready "by more than 63%", noted in ITER Organization.
More than 70% of the buildings have been completed, the installation of the first components of the reactor itself has begun.
The full phase of installation should begin next year, as the construction and delivery of all the necessary components: for example, China on September 23 built the first 400-ton magnetic coil, it will be delivered to the site of ITER construction by December.
In terms of complexity and manufacturability, ITER surpasses many large-scale scientific buildings of the century, including the Big Hadron Collider.
"A collider is just a vacuum plant that accelerates a bunch of protons, it's a simpler level task.
ITER is a physics of plasma, and plasma is so many degrees of freedom, so much instability, all of them need to be dealt with, - said Radio Svoboda, head of the Russian agency of the ITER project Anatoly Krasilnikov. - In terms of a large number of parameters that need to be taken into account at the same time, ITER, of course, is a much more complex problem than a collider.
Well, ITER is more expensive. "
Such a complex international project based on advanced technologies is really expensive.
If at the start the project budget was estimated at €5 billion, then by 2017 it had already reached the level of €20 billion: the total figure is difficult to estimate, as governments themselves determine the level of expenditure on certain components produced by them.
Participants of the project transfer not money, but transfer the built components.
In the Russian budget for ITER in 2020-22, 11.8 billion rubles (about $180 million) were invested.
Not only ITER, the Bublic-Tokomak is not the only option for thermonuclear synthesis considered by science.
Alternative ways are studied not only in large government institutions, but also in small startups.
They are now in the world, according to Bloomberg estimates, more than two dozen.
However, major breakthroughs and controlled commercial energy production have not yet been reported.
The nearest analogue of the current cell is a ratchet, also a toroidal, "bagle-like" system, with all its similarity does not require maintaining the current in the plasma.
Such an installation has its pros and cons, the largest and most successful at the moment - German Wendelstein 7-X.
On it, German researchers set a number of records, although in terms of characteristics and scale, it is far from ITER.
The Commonwealth Fusion Systems startup, based on MIT, promises to build a much smaller, cheaper, while slightly less efficient than ITER, SPARC.
How do they manage to do that?
Scientists hope to apply the latest high-temperature superconductors and are going to show solutions in the next two years.
Another non-standard option is thermonuclear synthesis with inertial holding.
It uses lasers on all sides "crimping" and heating the miniature fuel capsule deuterium pulses, imitating the processes occurring during the explosion of a hydrogen bomb.
The largest scientific organization in the world that applies this approach is the National Ignition Facility in the United States, where 193 beams of powerful lasers are used for this purpose.
Canadian General Fusion and American Tri Alpha Energy use their own, even more exotic methods of thermonuclear fusion, but alas, no one has yet introduced commercially ready solutions.
Why and when?
Critics believe that thermonuclear synthesis is too expensive and commercially inefficient, and they are encouraged to invest, for example, in renewable energy.
ITER does not deny its importance, but emphasizes that the creation of new clean energy sources with a constant generation level (independent of, say, the number of sunny days or wind power) remains an important task.
Thermonuclear energy will not replace renewable energy, but will serve together with it as an even better alternative to traditional "dirty" sources of energy, says ITER.
The only question is when it happens.
The first launch is planned for December 2025 ("the best technically achievable date") using hydrogen, then helium, deuterium will be added and finally full-fledged work on deuterium tritium is planned in 2035: only then can a tenfold recoil in power be achieved.
The project completion dates have already shifted, and given its complexity, it is unlikely that there will be no further delays.
In addition, despite all attempts, thermonuclear synthesis may be too expensive for industrial applications at the current stage of technology development.
Skeptics say that "thermo poison is the source of energy of the future, and will always remain so."
In a few years, humanity will be able to cool the fervor of skeptics or back up their positions.
Given the complexity of the topic, it is unlikely that someone is ready to guarantee deadlines in such projects.
One of the pioneers of the industry, the Soviet academician Lev Artsimovich, to the question of when the thermonuclear energy will appear, answered simply: "Then, when it becomes really necessary for humanity."
